content: Spirometra erinaceieuropaei is a parasitic tapeworm that infects both domestic animals and humans. In humans, the infection caused by this parasite is referred to as sparganosis. The lifecycle of Spirometra erinaceieuropaei begins when eggs from the adult worm are excreted in the feces of the definitive host. These eggs develop into procercoid larvae in the environment. Humans can become infected by directly ingesting these larvae, or the larvae may first infect an intermediate host, such as frogs, birds, snakes, rats, or mice, where they develop into plerocercoid larvae. If a definitive host, such as a cat, dog, fox, or wolf, consumes the intermediate host, the worm completes its lifecycle and matures into an adult capable of producing eggs. However, when humans ingest the parasite at the procercoid stage, they become a dead-end host, as the lifecycle cannot progress further in humans. The treatment of sparganosis primarily involves surgical intervention. The preferred approach is the surgical removal of subcutaneous masses caused by the parasite or the injection of ethanol into these masses. While praziquantel, administered at a dose of 75 mg/kg/day orally for three days, has been used in some cases, its efficacy is controversial. It has shown limited success in certain patients and is generally considered less effective compared to surgical therapy. However, in situations where surgery is not feasible, praziquantel may be considered as an alternative treatment option.
